statement: In a cohort of 96 women in the United Kingdom recruited in pregnancy through midwives, leaflets and magazine advertisements asking for women who used recreational drugs, 28 had used MDMA in the month before or during pregnancy (mostly in the first 3 months: on average 1.61 tablets a week in the month before pregnancy, 0.82 in the first 3 months, 0.08 in the second 3 months and 0.006 in the last, with a median of 0.13 a week across pregnancy; one woman used in the last 3 months; tablet contents were not tested) and 68 had not (32 of them had used before). At about 1 month (22 exposed and 60 comparison infants) no mean neurobehavioral score differed (two shifts in the spread of scores, toward more lethargic and less rigid behaviour, reached P<0.07). At 4 months (22 and 65 infants) the Bayley mental (99.1 against 98.6) and psychomotor (96.5 against 94.3) scores and the Alberta motor scale percentile (50.4 against 45.8; 14% below the 10th percentile in both groups) did not differ, but an assessor-rated motor quality score was lower in exposed infants (58.9 against 74.1, P=0.009) and still lower after adjusting for alcohol (beta -0.21, P<0.05); exposed infants were more often boys (71% against 46%; adjusted odds ratio 3.2, 95% CI 1.2 to 8.2) (Singer et al., 2012). The women who used MDMA also used more cocaine (71% against 16% of women), cannabis, tobacco and amphetamine and more alcohol (9.1 against 6.6 units a week), fathers were not asked, and these are among many scores tested without correction in small groups, so the study cannot separate MDMA from the other exposures. The authors' dose-response rests on infants of the 13 women with heavier use scoring lower than infants of the 15 women with lighter use, while infants of the lighter-use group scored above the unexposed on two scales. Development after 4 months and exposure beyond the first 3 months were not studied.
plain: One study followed babies of women who used ecstasy in pregnancy, mostly in the first 3 months: on average about 1.6 tablets a week in the month before pregnancy and 0.8 a week in the first 3 months. At 1 month, average scores in 22 exposed babies and 60 others did not differ, though two patterns leaned toward more low-energy behavior (91 in 100 against 73 in 100) and less stiffness (9 against 27); neither passed the usual cut-off. At 4 months, standard mental and movement tests were also about the same. One rating of movement quality was lower in exposed babies (average score 59 against 74), and more of them were boys (71 in 100 against 46 in 100). The mothers also used more cocaine, cannabis, tobacco and alcohol, so the study cannot tell which drug mattered. The babies were followed only to 4 months.
population: Infants of 96 UK women recruited in pregnancy because they used recreational drugs: 28 exposed to MDMA in the month before or during pregnancy (22 seen at 1 and at 4 months) and 68 not exposed (60 seen at 1 month, 65 at 4 months)
exposure: Self-reported MDMA use in the month before or during pregnancy, mostly in the first 3 months (mean 1.61 tablets a week in the month before, 0.82 in the first 3 months), with no biological check and no testing of tablet contents
comparator: Infants of women who used recreational drugs but not MDMA in pregnancy (32 had used before pregnancy)
outcome: Neonatal behaviour at about 1 month (NNNS); Bayley mental and psychomotor scores, behaviour-rating motor quality and attention, and Alberta motor percentile at 4 months; birth measures and sex
magnitude: 1 month (22 against 60): no mean NNNS score differed (lethargy 3.14 against 2.63, P=.22). 4 months (22 against 65): Bayley mental 99.1 against 98.6 (P=.80); psychomotor 96.5 against 94.3 (P=.40); Alberta percentile 50.4 against 45.8 (P=.51), 14% below the 10th percentile in both; behaviour-rating motor quality 58.9 (SD 20.7) against 74.1 (23.8), t -2.61, P=.009, adjusted beta -.21 (P<.05) after alcohol. Three groups (none, lighter, heavier): motor quality 74.1, 60.8, 57.0 (P<.04); Alberta percentile 45.9, 65.7, 35.1 (P<.03); psychomotor 94.3, 101.1, 91.8 (P<.08). Male births 20 of 28 (71%) against 31 of 68 (46%), adjusted odds ratio 3.2 (95% CI 1.2 to 8.2). Other drugs in the exposed group: cocaine 71% against 16%, cannabis 82% against 54%, tobacco 86% against 62%.

evidence.locator: 2. Methods > 2.1.1 Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; 2.1.2 Measures of MDMA Exposure and Covariates, 1st paragraph; 2.1.2.1 Prenatal Levels of Drug Exposure, 1st paragraph; 2.1.4 Statistical Analyses, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Recruitment of pregnant women who had used recreational drugs through midwives, leaflets at prenatal clinics and advertisements in pregnancy magazines (ecstasy, tobacco, cannabis, alcohol and cocaine named as examples); 126 responded, 5 did not meet criteria, 25 did not come to the first visit, leaving 96; 82 infants were seen at about 1 month and 87 at 4 months. Women were classed as exposed if they said they used MDMA during pregnancy or in the month before (28); women who had used earlier but not then (32) and women who had never used were the comparison (68 in all). 62 women were interviewed during pregnancy and 24 after birth; use was by self-report with no biological check.

evidence.locator: 3. Results > 3.1 Maternal Outcomes, 3rd to 7th paragraphs; Tables 2 and 4
evidence.extracted: Mean tablets a week for the 28 exposed women (Table 4): month before pregnancy 1.61 (SD 3.11), first trimester 0.82 (1.58), second 0.08 (0.38), third 0.006 (0.03); one woman used in the third trimester. Table 2: over pregnancy mean 0.6 (SD 1.1), median 0.13 (range 0.01 to 4.5). The text gives 3.2 tablets a week (SD 5.2) before pregnancy 'for those who used MDMA during pregnancy' and a mean total of 25 tablets over pregnancy and the month before (SD 43.7, range 0.45 to 180). Median split (0.14 a week): heavier 13 women, lighter 15; they differed mainly in the month before pregnancy (3.3 against 0.12 tablets a week, P<.007) and less in the first trimester (1.6 against 0.12, P<.12).

evidence.locator: 3. Results > 3.1 Maternal Outcomes, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Tables 1 to 3
evidence.extracted: The women who used MDMA were more likely to use cocaine (71% against 16% of women), cannabis (82% against 54%), tobacco (86% against 62%), amphetamine (18% against 3%), mushrooms (14% against none), LSD (11% against none) and ketamine (7% against none) in pregnancy, and used more alcohol (9.1 against 6.6 units a week; 96% against 91% of women); they had fewer previous births (parity 1.21 against 1.88) and higher drug-problem scores (DAST 7.7 against 4.6). The groups were similar in age, education, income, ethnicity and two intelligence subtests.

evidence.locator: 3. Results > 3.2 Birth and Neonatal Child Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Table 5
evidence.extracted: All births were singletons. No group difference in gestation (40.0 against 39.5 weeks), birth weight (3537 against 3344 g), prematurity (1 of 28 against 1 of 68), length or head circumference (the last two with many missing values). Exposed infants were more often male: 20 of 28 (71%) against 31 of 68 (46%), chi-square 5.32, P=0.02; odds ratio of a male birth 3.2 (95% CI 1.2 to 8.2, P<.02) after controlling for other drug differences. The authors state that they cannot establish whether the sex-ratio difference is caused by MDMA.

evidence.locator: 3. Results > 3.3 Neonatal Behavioral Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Table 6
evidence.extracted: NNNS at about 1 month (22 exposed, 60 comparison infants; mean age 33.6 days): no mean score differed (for example lethargy 3.14 against 2.63, P=.22; excitability 1.64 against 2.35, P=.15); trends in the score distributions for more lethargic behaviour (91% against 73%) and less hypertonicity (9% against 27%), both P<.069.

evidence.locator: 3. Results > 3.4 Child Outcomes at 4-Months-Old, 1st paragraph; Table 7
evidence.extracted: At 4 months (22 exposed, 65 comparison infants): Bayley mental index 99.1 (SD 6.4) against 98.6 (8.9), P=.80; psychomotor index 96.5 (10.0) against 94.3 (10.8), P=.40; behaviour-rating attention/arousal 71.2 against 70.9; Alberta motor scale percentile 50.4 against 45.8, P=.51, with 14% below the 10th percentile in both groups; behaviour-rating motor quality 58.9 (SD 20.7) against 74.1 (23.8), t -2.61, P=.009. After controlling for average alcohol exposure, MDMA still predicted poorer motor quality (beta -.21, P<.05); average tablets a week over pregnancy predicted it too (beta -.24, P<.042).

evidence.locator: 3. Results > 3.4 Child Outcomes at 4-Months-Old, 2nd paragraph; Table 8; 3.5 Other Drug Effects, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Three-group comparison at 4 months (none, lighter, heavier): behaviour-rating motor quality 74.1, 60.8, 57.0 (F 3.6, P<.04); Alberta percentile 45.9, 65.7, 35.1 (F 3.8, P<.03); psychomotor index 94.3, 101.1, 91.8 (P<.08); below the 10th percentile 14%, 0 and 27% (P<.18), so the lighter group scored above the unexposed on the psychomotor index and the Alberta percentile. Higher alcohol exposure predicted poorer motor quality (beta -.36, P<.005), and higher cannabis exposure poorer attention (beta -.28) and regulation (beta -.27) at 1 month (both P<.02).

Limitations the authors state: voluntary enrolment, self-reported use that may be unreliable, fetal exposure almost entirely in the first trimester, a small exposed sample, and fathers' use not asked. They conclude that the findings suggest risk to the developing child and warrant follow-up of the cohort to see whether the early motor differences persist or resolve. The abstract and highlights say exposed infants had poorer motor quality and lower milestone attainment, with a dose-response relationship; in the group comparison the Bayley psychomotor and Alberta scores did not differ.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E high on the study card: the exposed women used much more cocaine, cannabis, tobacco and alcohol, fathers' use and weight gain are unknown; self-reported exposure; differential follow-up (79% against 88 to 96%); many outcomes without correction, and an abstract that features the significant ones.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for UK women who used recreational drugs, mostly in the first 3 months, and infants to 4 months.

imprecision.note: 22 exposed infants; the three-group comparison rests on about 11 infants per group.

grade.reasoning: An observational cohort starts low (METHODS 6.3); risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. Status single-study. The claim lists the null results first and the associations with their confounding, so it says no more than the anchors show; it is not a statement about cause or about any amount.

verification.flag_note: Joins with the claim on birth defects (same exposure). Reference record singer_2012 is metadata-verified; the cohort's later follow-up (beyond 4 months) was not found in the library's reference list.
